title: Whose Knowledge Shapes the Decision?
audience: Staff examining evidence and participation in service or workforce decisions; supervisors and managers considering whose contribution receives meaningful consideration.

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Whose Knowledge Shapes the Decision?
Examine credibility, categories, and influence so relevant knowledge can enter a decision without losing the person’s meaning.
Advanced self-directed learning
slides.narration: An organization can invite people to speak and still leave their knowledge outside its decisions. This course examines how that happens through credibility judgments, reporting categories, and the route from a contribution to an actual choice. You will follow service, workplace, and community examples. The aim is not to accept every account without examination. It is to apply relevant evidence questions fairly, preserve the meaning and ownership of contributions, and identify practical responses when a familiar title or vocabulary determines whose concern is taken seriously.

slides.text:
The same concern, a different reception
A service user describes a confusing handoff. The concern is dismissed as misunderstanding. A professional repeats the same concern, and it receives attention.

Ask what changed: the evidence, the explanation, or the speaker’s standing? The comparison invites inquiry; it does not establish motive.
slides.narration: Pause with the two responses. A professional may add relevant evidence, but the practice example says the same concern is repeated. The useful question is why the original account did not receive substantive examination. A title can make information easier to hear while quietly becoming a substitute for evidence. Repeating that pattern may keep people with direct experience dependent on a higher-status messenger. Examine the actual account and reception without inferring a private motive or assuming every difference in response proves injustice.

slides.text:
A wrong in how knowledge is received
Fricker describes unfair credibility discounts and unequal access to the shared understanding used to explain experience.

In plain terms: someone’s account may receive less consideration, or the available categories may fail to describe it. Both need evidence in the particular situation.
slides.narration: The concept of epistemic injustice concerns people as contributors of knowledge. One form involves an unfair credibility discount; another concerns an unequal ability to make experience understandable within shared categories. These concepts help you ask a sharper organizational question without diagnosing every exchange. A service user’s account can be relevant but incomplete, just as a specialist’s account can be relevant but limited. The remedy is fair examination and a usable route into reasoning, rather than ranking people once and letting that rank decide every claim.

slides.text:
Worked comparison: receive the substance
Option A: require a professional to confirm the person’s concern before examining it.

Option B: record the actual concern, ask relevant clarifying questions, and examine the route using the same evidence standard.

B preserves inquiry without making status the gate. The concern’s wider cause remains open.
slides.narration: A professional can contribute expertise without becoming the price of admission for someone else’s knowledge. Option B asks what happened, what information supports the account, and which explanations remain. Those questions can strengthen the inquiry while respecting the original contribution. If Option A is repeated, concerns from people without a sponsor may never enter the review. The comparison does not require accepting the account as a complete finding. It offers a fairer way to examine it and preserves the possibility that further evidence changes the explanation.

slides.text:
A concern waits for a professional voice
In this example, a service user describes a confusing handoff. Review begins only after a professional repeats the same concern. What should the equity analysis examine?
A. Whether the user’s title and vocabulary were sufficiently professional.
B. The original substance, changed reception, and evidence standard, preserving the account’s meaning.
C. The professional’s repetition proves intentional discrimination.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The practice sequence supplies the same concern and a change in its reception. It does not establish private motives or a population pattern. Consider which response examines the knowledge gate rather than the person’s presentation or a conclusion the evidence cannot support. The original account may be incomplete and still deserve relevant questions. Repeatedly requiring a higher-status messenger can keep direct service experience from shaping the work. Choose a response that preserves the meaning, examines the standard, and compares a practical route while respecting actual responsibilities.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Whether the user’s title and vocabulary were sufficiently professional.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. The original substance, changed reception, and evidence standard, preserving the account’s meaning.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. The professional’s repetition proves intentional discrimination.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A title is not evidence of the handoff. Repeated credibility gates can keep direct experience outside decisions. Examine the concern with relevant questions; its cause and wider distribution remain unknown.

Would the same evidence question be asked if a different person supplied the concern?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Professional vocabulary may make a concern familiar, but it does not establish whether the handoff worked. Making that vocabulary the entry condition can repeatedly keep direct knowledge out of review. A better response records the substance and asks relevant clarifying questions using a consistent standard. The supplied sequence does not settle motive, cause, or the distribution of similar experiences.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Examine what changed and apply fair evidence questions. Repeated status gates may filter service knowledge. Preserve the original account and compare a usable route; motive, cause, and wider effects are not established.

Would the same evidence question be asked if a different person supplied the concern?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: This response examines the original contribution and the changed reception without requiring either automatic acceptance or a status sponsor. Repeated credibility gates can filter which service concerns reach decisions. Compare a route that applies relevant evidence questions and preserves the person’s meaning. The sequence supports inquiry while wider effects, intent, and formal findings remain separate unanswered questions.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
The sequence supports inquiry, not a finding of intent. Repeated status gates may matter, but examine relevant comparisons and alternatives. Keep the account faithful and formal findings within their actual process.

Would the same evidence question be asked if a different person supplied the concern?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A different reception is relevant, but it cannot alone establish deliberate discrimination. That claim needs fitting evidence and the actual process. Preserve the original concern and examine the credibility standard, relevant comparisons, and possible explanations. A supported design response can address a gate without overstating intent or replacing a formal concern procedure.

slides.text:
Test the claim rather than the identity
Ask what was observed, which records or conditions matter, and what would support or challenge the account.

Do not replace these questions with an impression of confidence, education, accent, disability, race, or position. Relevant expertise answers a question; status does not answer every question.
slides.narration: Expertise matters when it fits the question. A person using a service can explain the burden they encountered, an analyst can examine a relevant pattern, and a specialist can interpret a requirement. None automatically supplies the entire explanation. Compare how similar claims are questioned and retained. A credibility discount can recur without an explicit rule when familiar speech is heard as knowledge and unfamiliar speech as confusion. A better response separates the substance from an impression of the speaker and keeps alternative explanations available.

slides.text:
The category can lose the sequence
A reporting form offers “technical problem” or “staff conduct.” A person describes an unusable page followed by a dismissive response.

Forcing one category may erase part of the account. Preserve valid definitions while examining a route for the sequence they do not capture.
slides.narration: Categories make information manageable, but they can also narrow what the organization sees. The account spans a technical condition and its reception. Selecting only one may send the concern to a contact who cannot understand the complete sequence. Repeating that restriction can make a recurring barrier appear absent. The response is not to discard every category or create a new label without thought. Examine whether relevant detail can reach the appropriate review through actual responsibilities while preserving technical meanings and the person’s account.

slides.text:
Silence is not a supplied opinion
A person may be listening, preparing, tired, uncertain, or judging the setting unsuitable. None is established by silence alone.

Invite a relevant contribution through usable routes. Do not require personal disclosure or a public performance to demonstrate commitment.
slides.narration: A meeting can record who spoke without knowing why someone did not. Turning that observation into an employee label carries the record beyond its evidence. A thoughtful invitation focuses on the work and explains what remains open to influence. It may offer a considered response route rather than require immediate speech. Repeatedly rewarding only visible airtime can narrow the knowledge used in decisions and later development. Preserve the person’s choice about private reflection while making an actual opportunity to contribute understandable and usable.

slides.text:
Different sources answer different questions
A contact log can count acknowledgments. A person can explain an earlier attempt or whether the acknowledgment clarified the next action.

Keep both within scope. A count does not disprove a different experience, and an account does not automatically describe every record.
slides.narration: The apparent disagreement may concern different questions. A log begins at a recorded request, while a person describes an earlier call. Both can be accurate. Compare the definitions and sequence before selecting one as the true account. An analyst can help explain the record, and lived experience can identify what it omits. If only the easiest measure repeatedly enters the decision, earlier barriers may stay invisible. Integration means making the relationship among sources clear, not treating every story as a population finding or every count as complete experience.

slides.text:
Worked comparison: recognition at work
In this example, an employee proposes a useful change. It receives little attention until a senior colleague repeats it and receives credit.

Compare the original contribution, its later reception, and the record of recognition. Credit can shape access to development and future evidence of readiness.
slides.narration: Recognition matters beyond the moment because visible contribution can lead to assignments, sponsorship, and advancement evidence. The practice sequence supplies an original idea and a later repetition. It does not prove anyone intended to take credit or establish every employee’s experience. Examine how the substantive contribution was recorded and why its reception changed. A consistent way to preserve attribution and evaluate the idea may address the gate. Follow the connection across onboarding, supervision, development, and advancement without judging private motives or requiring the employee to confront colleagues publicly.

slides.text:
Credit travels to the repeated idea
In this example, an employee’s proposal receives attention after a senior colleague repeats it and receives credit. Which response best addresses the possible opportunity effect?
A. Preserve attribution, examine the proposal fairly, and clarify how recognition enters later development evidence.
B. Tell the employee to speak more forcefully next time.
C. Require the employee to share a personal identity story at the next meeting.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: Recognition can influence who receives assignments and whose work later appears as evidence of readiness. In the practice sequence, an employee’s proposal receives attention after a senior colleague repeats it and is credited. The example does not establish anyone’s intent or the employee’s future outcome. Consider a response that addresses the account and how it enters later decisions rather than asking the employee to perform confidence or disclose identity. A practical correction preserves the substantive proposal and attribution through actual responsibilities. Choose the response that examines the recurring opportunity pathway.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Preserve attribution, examine the proposal fairly, and clarify how recognition enters later development evidence.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Tell the employee to speak more forcefully next time.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Require the employee to share a personal identity story at the next meeting.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Correct the account and examine its use. Repeated lost credit can shape assignments and later readiness evidence. Compare a faithful recognition route; motives and advancement results remain unknown.

Which later opportunity could depend on the way a contribution is recorded?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A faithful record can address the knowledge failure and help colleagues examine the proposal on its merits. If lost credit repeatedly affects assignment access, it may shape later evidence for development or advancement. Clarify the relevant route without inventing authority to reopen every decision. Motives, individual competence, and later promotion results remain unknown in this practice example.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A stronger performance does not repair the account. Repeatedly placing the burden on the speaker can preserve the credibility gate. Examine attribution and evidence instead; the employee’s commitment is not supplied.

Which later opportunity could depend on the way a contribution is recorded?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: Speaking more forcefully may be the employee’s choice, but it does not correct attribution or explain why the idea’s reception changed. Repeatedly making the speaker carry that burden can preserve a credibility gate. Examine the actual proposal, record, and recognition route instead. The scenario supplies no basis to rate the employee’s confidence, willingness, or competence.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Private disclosure is not a condition for proper credit. Repeating that demand can add burden and restrict participation. Preserve the contribution and chosen use through actual roles; identity does not prove the proposal.

Which later opportunity could depend on the way a contribution is recorded?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A personal identity story is not required to receive fair consideration or accurate credit. Demanding it can repeatedly add another burden to participation and expose information the employee did not choose to share. Preserve the work contribution and clarify its chosen use through actual responsibilities. The substantive idea can be examined without using identity as evidence of its quality.

slides.text:
Influence needs an open choice
Explain which question is being examined, what remains open, and how relevant knowledge can enter before the choice closes.

An option to comment after the decision may support understanding, but it does not give the contribution influence over that already settled choice.
slides.narration: An invitation can be warm and still arrive too late for its stated purpose. If a decision is settled, explain that honestly and identify any question still open. When a choice is open, provide the needed material and a usable route for relevant contributions to reach the review. Repeating invitations without influence can make participation feel extractive. That concern does not establish that every suggestion must be adopted. It asks whether the knowledge can affect the reasoning and whether people receive an understandable account of the response.

slides.text:
Preserve meaning and chosen attribution
Summarize the substance without adding a personality label, identity narrative, or representative role.

Clarify how the account may be used and credited through the actual arrangement. Public recognition is not automatically the repair a person wants.
slides.narration: A contribution about unclear wording can become a misleading story about shy employees finding their voice. That retelling changes both the question and the person’s role. A faithful summary identifies the task issue and the response, while preserving what the person chooses to share. Recognition may be helpful, but someone may prefer a private correction or no public story. Repeatedly taking over meaning can weaken trust and discourage useful knowledge. Clarify actual use and attribution rather than assuming inclusion gives unlimited permission to publish an account.

slides.text:
A correction must reach the next decision
Correct an inaccurate summary or lost attribution through the appropriate arrangement. Explain where the correction changes the reasoning.

An apology can matter without repairing the record or the opportunity. No one must forgive or join a learning discussion to receive a proper response.
slides.narration: If the knowledge failure changed the record, a conversation alone may leave that record influencing future choices. Examine what repair is possible within actual responsibilities, including a faithful account or a reconsideration where appropriate. The course does not supply authority to reopen a formal decision or investigate a complaint. It helps identify the consequence worth addressing. Keep required processes in place and avoid making repair conditional on the person’s willingness to share more. A practical correction should address the relevant route, not merely improve the tone of the exchange.

slides.text:
Community briefs prepare; people contribute
Use a culture brief to prepare respectful questions and notice assumptions about meaning or participation.

Actual contributors provide their own accounts. No brief, partner, or employee represents everyone. Invite disagreement and clarify what can influence the decision.
slides.narration: Preparation can help staff hear a concern without requiring people to explain every background term. A culture brief may prompt a useful question about support or communication. It cannot establish an individual’s experience or convert a participant into a spokesperson for a whole community. Explain how the account enters the decision and preserve differing meanings. Repeatedly selecting only the most familiar account can narrow the knowledge base even when attendance looks diverse. A substantive invitation welcomes relevant challenge while keeping the evidence and participation conditions clear.

slides.text:
Compare routes from knowledge to decision
Compare the baseline, a better invitation, and a route that also preserves substance, attribution, and timely consideration.

Consider access, influence, burden, evidence quality, and feasibility. More comments do not establish a better decision or a repaired credibility pattern.
slides.narration: A new response channel may widen entry while leaving the decision route unchanged. A more complete alternative explains the question, receives relevant accounts, preserves their meaning, and shows how they were considered. Compare it with the existing approach and necessary requirements. The consultant can support substantive inquiry without owning every decision or replacing specialist expertise. Unknown effects remain open. The strongest proposal addresses the identified knowledge gate and offers a practical way to examine its use rather than promising trust or better decisions from a larger comment count.

slides.text:
A category cannot hold the account
A community participant describes an unusable page followed by a dismissive response. In this example, a form accepts only “technical” or “conduct.” What is the strongest proposal?
A. Choose one category and discard the rest of the sequence.
B. Add a new label and declare the knowledge problem solved.
C. Preserve valid definitions and a usable route for the complete account to reach relevant review.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: The form offers two categories that each capture part of the participant’s account. The useful question is whether the sequence can reach an appropriate review without losing its meaning. A culture brief could help staff prepare thoughtful questions, but it cannot choose the category or make the person representative of everyone. Repeatedly erasing the interaction can leave the organization with an incomplete account of the barrier. Choose a proposal that preserves necessary definitions and a usable route, while keeping formal responsibilities and the results of any change in their actual scope.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Choose one category and discard the rest of the sequence.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Add a new label and declare the knowledge problem solved.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Preserve valid definitions and a usable route for the complete account to reach relevant review.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
One category may erase the interaction. Repeating that loss can keep the barrier outside review. Preserve the complete substance and examine the actual route; the concern’s cause and wider effects remain unknown.

What part of an account disappears when it must fit only one category?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A category may support a valid task, yet selecting only one here loses part of the supplied sequence. Repeating that loss can make an interaction appear absent from organizational evidence. Preserve the substantive account and examine how relevant detail reaches review through actual responsibilities. The learning example does not establish the cause of the response or wider distribution of similar concerns.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A label alone does not establish reception or response. Repeated unexamined categories may still lose the account. Compare a usable route and actual responsibilities; no solved outcome is supplied.

What part of an account disappears when it must fit only one category?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A new label may be useful, but it does not itself establish that anyone receives, understands, or responds to the account. Repeating the same route under a different name can preserve the original gate. Compare a practical way to retain the sequence and explain its actual destination. Keep the proposed repair separate from evidence that it has resolved the problem.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Retain the sequence and necessary definitions together. Repeated category gaps can filter knowledge. Examine a feasible route with actual responsibilities and chosen use; cause, prevalence, and the change’s effects remain open.

What part of an account disappears when it must fit only one category?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This proposal keeps valid definitions while making room for information they do not contain. A category gap can repeatedly prevent a connected concern from entering reasoning. Examine the route with actual responsibilities, preserve the contributor’s meaning and chosen use, and consider evidence of reception. The broader cause, prevalence, and effect of a future change remain questions to examine.

slides.text:
A useful explanation of the knowledge gap
Describe the account, reception, category or route, and consequence. State the relevant comparison and alternative explanations.

Recommend a feasible repair with actual responsibilities preserved. Distinguish the observed sequence from motive, wider distribution, and a legal finding.
slides.narration: A supported explanation names the knowledge lost and the place it should have informed the work. In the service case, the account concerns a handoff and receives attention only after repetition by a professional. That sequence supports examining the credibility gate. It does not establish why every reviewer responded as they did. A concrete recommendation might preserve the original concern and apply the same relevant questions. Explain what the repair addresses and which wider effects remain unknown, so colleagues can assess the reasoning rather than accept a slogan about listening.

slides.text:
Examine whether the route actually changes
Look for faithful summaries, substantive responses, and timely consideration through permitted evidence.

A rise or fall in comments does not explain itself. It may involve access, trust, need, or other conditions. Examine the route and experience rather than rating speakers’ willingness.
slides.narration: An improved route may produce more concerns because people can now contribute, or fewer because a practical barrier changed. Neither trend chooses its own explanation. Examine what the records show and what people describe, retaining limits and missing perspectives. Do not turn participation into a score for individual staff or demand that someone trust the process again. The organizational question is whether relevant knowledge can reach a decision and receive a meaningful response. That focus helps sustain a useful change without treating counts as proof of inclusion.

slides.text:
Rewrite a story that takes over meaning
Original: “Our quiet employees needed a senior voice to explain their needs.”

Supported: “An employee identified a handoff concern. The same concern received review after a senior colleague repeated it.”

What correction would preserve the original contribution and address the route?
slides.narration: Try your own revision before reading the example. The first sentence assigns a personality, a need, and a representative role that the account does not establish. The supported revision retains the contribution and the changed reception. It opens a question about the route rather than turning the employee into a learning example. Consider what correction would matter to the actual record and future opportunity. A more faithful explanation can make a recurring credibility pattern visible while keeping motives, wider experience, and appropriate formal responsibilities separate.

slides.text:
Reflect on whose words you hear first
Consider a time when a title, confident delivery, or familiar language made an account easier to accept. What evidence did you examine?

Keep your reflection private. Identify one way to ask fairer questions without dismissing either expertise or lived experience.
slides.narration: Most people rely on familiar cues to understand a complicated exchange. Reflection can help you notice when those cues have become a shortcut for credibility. You do not need to disclose a personal story or name someone whose account you received. Consider whether the same substantive concern would have entered your reasoning from a different speaker. The aim is not self-condemnation or an individual development score. It is a more thoughtful relationship between evidence, expertise, direct experience, and the practical route by which knowledge influences work.

slides.text:
A fair route for relevant knowledge
Receive the substance, examine the evidence, preserve meaning, and make timely consideration possible.

Relevant expertise and particular experience contribute different knowledge. Repair the specific gate, keep actual responsibilities, and examine whether the next decision can hear what the earlier one missed.
slides.narration: A useful decision needs more than an invitation to speak. It needs relevant knowledge to enter the reasoning without an unfair credibility gate or a category that erases the experience. Preserve rigorous questions and the person’s meaning together. A practical repair can improve a record, an invitation, or the route to consideration without promising every contribution will determine the result. That approach supports service understanding and employee opportunity while keeping unknown motives, wider effects, and formal responsibilities in their actual places.

outcomes: Identify a credibility discount in how an account is received or recorded.
Explain how available categories can leave an experience undescribed.
Design a route by which an affected person’s contribution can influence a decision.
Recommend a repair that preserves the person’s meaning and ownership of the account.
